common_conventions: Decisions at close d using only data released by d (FRED daily series are taken as of d-1 because they publish with a one-business-day lag; monthly macro series as of their release date); engine exec=next_close; returns are daily excess over T-bill; positions without natural sizing are scaled to 10% annualised ex-ante vol with EWMA (com 60) of the instrument's daily excess returns using data to d, gross notional cap 4 unless stated; realistic one-way costs per the task map (ES 1bp, ZN 1bp, ZT 0.5, ZF 0.7, ZB/UB 1.5, FX 1, CL/GC/SI/HG 2, NG/HO/RB/PL 3, grains/livestock 4, ETFs config.cost_bps + 30bp/yr borrow on shorts), 2x as stress. At most 3 pre-declared variants each (A is the primary).

candidates.name: VIX/VIX3M term-structure equity timing
sources: Johnson (2017) JFQA, Risk Premia and the VIX Term Structure, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2548050
Fassas & Hourvouliades (2019) JRFM 12(3):113, VIX Futures as a Market Timing Indicator, https://www.mdpi.com/1911-8074/12/3/113
Practitioner episode statistics 2010-2026, https://www.thetrading.tools/manuals/vix-term-structure
candidates.exact_rule: Daily. R_d = ^VIX close / ^VIX3M close at d. Base = long F_ES at 10% ex-ante vol. A (risk-off): weight = base if R_d < 1.00, else 0 (T-bills). B (contrarian, Fassas-Hourvouliades): weight = 1.5 x base if R_d >= 1.00, else base. C (persistent backwardation): weight 0 only if R >= 1.00 on each of the last 5 sessions, else base. exec next_close.
candidates.data_needed: index_daily ^VIX, ^VIX3M (2006-07+); futures_daily F_ES; rf_daily
candidates.external_evidence: Fassas-Hourvouliades (VIX futures 2010-2017): backwardation followed by positive S&P returns, significant at daily/weekly/quarterly horizons and stronger at longer horizons; contango carries no signal (i.e. evidence favours B over A). Practitioner tally 2010-2026: 63 backwardation episodes (8% of days, about 5 days each); SPY +3.9% over the next quarter from the first day (75% positive) vs +3.2% all-day baseline, but long-lasting backwardation (2011, 2018, 2020) coincided with real drawdowns (motivates C). Johnson: slope summarises the price of variance risk (variance-asset returns), not a published net equity-timing record. No live/net record found.
candidates.adaptation_note: Source sample 2010-2017 sits inside our in-sample window (not independent). VIX3M replaces VIX futures slope. A and B are opposite bets; both pre-declared, choose on IS only.

candidates.name: Variance-risk-premium equity timing (VIX^2 minus realised variance)
sources: Bollerslev, Tauchen & Zhou (2009) RFS 22(11), Expected Stock Returns and Variance Risk Premia, https://papers.ssrn.com/abstract=948309

Byun, Frijns & Roh (2018) JFM 38(4), A comprehensive look at the return predictability of variance risk premia, https://research.ou.nl/en/publications/a-comprehensive-look-at-the-return-predictability-of-variance-ris/
Goyal, Welch & Zafirov (2024) RFS 37(11), https://www.ivo-welch.org/home/card-eqpredict.html
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at last session d of the month. VRP_d = (VIX_d/100)^2 - RV_d, RV_d = (252/21) * sum of squared daily F_ES excess log returns over the last 21 sessions. Weight in units of the 10%-vol F_ES base: A = 1.0 if VRP_d > median of month-end VRP over the trailing 60 months (min 36) else 0.5. B = clip(1 + 0.5 z, 0, 1.5), z = (VRP_d - trailing 60m mean)/trailing 60m sd. C (BTZ regression) = expanding OLS (min 60 monthly obs; VIXCLS and S&P history from 1990) of next-3-month S&P excess return on VRP, weight = clip(mu_hat_ann / (3 sigma2_ann), 0, 1.5) with sigma2 from trailing 252 sessions.
candidates.data_needed: VIXCLS (FRED 1990+) or ^VIX; F_ES TR; ^GSPC 1990-2002 via yfinance for the regression history; rf
candidates.external_evidence: BTZ (1990-2007): high VRP predicts high returns, strongest at the quarterly horizon and dominant over P/E, default spread and cay. Byun-Frijns-Roh (2018): strong out-of-sample predictability for the US index, FX and credit, profitable real-time timing (no bonds/commodities). Counter: Goyal-Welch-Zafirov (2024, data to 2021) do not list BTZ among the few predictors that still work in- and out-of-sample.
candidates.adaptation_note: Daily squared ES returns replace 5-minute realised variance (hourly ES bars could be used for a 1-hour RV). Monthly decision, quarterly-horizon signal.

candidates.name: Connors VIX stretch mean reversion on the S&P
candidates.family: volatility regime - short-term VIX spike reversal
sources: Connors & Alvarez (2008) Short Term Trading Strategies That Work (book), notes: https://www.cxoadvisory.com/technical-trading/a-few-notes-on-short-term-trading-strategies-that-work/
candidates.exact_rule: Daily. Setup at close d: ^GSPC close > its 200-session SMA AND on each of sessions d-2, d-1, d the VIX close >= 1.05 x its own 10-session SMA. Enter long F_ES (10% ex-ante vol sizing) at next_close; exit at the next close after the first close where 2-period Wilder RSI of the ES TR index > 65. Flat otherwise. A = as stated. B = A plus a 10-session time stop. C = A with a 1.10 stretch threshold.
candidates.data_needed: index_daily ^VIX, ^GSPC; futures_daily F_ES
candidates.external_evidence: Book backtests on SPY/S&P about 1993-2007 with high win rates, gross, no independent net record verified; Connors-family short-term S&P reversal rules are widely replicated in blogs but decay is reported after 2010.
candidates.adaptation_note: Source enters at the signal-day close; our engine fills at the next close (one-day lag reduces edge). Low exposure (in market a small share of days).

candidates.name: Moreira-Muir volatility-managed ES (1/realised variance)
sources: Moreira & Muir (2017) JF, Volatility-Managed Portfolios, https://www.nber.org/papers/22208
Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan (2020) JFE, https://www.lehigh.edu/~xuy219/research/COWY.pdf
Wang & Yan (2021) JBF 131:106198, https://www.lehigh.edu/~xuy219/research/Downside.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at month-end d. RV_m = 252 x mean of squared daily F_ES excess returns over the sessions of the month ending d. A: w = 0.10 sigma_LR / RV_m (sigma_LR = trailing 2520-session RMS vol, min 252), cap 1.5 x 0.10/sigma_LR. B: w = c / RV_m with c reset each month so the expanding-sample mean weight equals the static weight 0.10/sigma_LR (real-time MM normalisation), cap 1.5x static. C: rule A applied to the equal-risk ES+ZN sleeve (portfolio RV). exec next_close, engine re-trades daily to target.
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily F_ES, F_ZN; rf
candidates.external_evidence: MM 1926-2015: market alpha 4.86%/yr, beta about 0.6, Sharpe up, robust to a 1.5x leverage cap. Cederburg et al. (2020): real-time versions underperform the unmanaged portfolio in 72 of 103 equity strategies. Wang-Yan real-time (expanding, 120m training) market: combination 0.48 vs unmanaged 0.46 Sharpe (n.s.).
candidates.adaptation_note: Variant A is the same rule as the edge-search series rpm_ES_MM (scratchpad/edges/series/rpm_ES_MM.parquet), which has no verifier verdict in the journal yet; reuse it once verified instead of recomputing.

candidates.name: Downside-volatility-managed ES
sources: Wang & Yan (2021) JBF 131:106198, Downside risk and the performance of volatility-managed portfolios, https://www.lehigh.edu/~xuy219/research/Downside.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at month-end d. sigma_down = sqrt(252/N x sum over the month's N sessions of r_j^2 for r_j < 0) of daily F_ES excess returns (if fewer than 3 negative days, use the last two months). A: w = 0.10 x k / sigma_down, k = trailing 2520-session (min 252) median of monthly sigma_total/sigma_down so the weight is unbiased, cap 2 x static. B (fixed-weight combination recommended by the source): 0.5 x A + 0.5 x static (0.10/sigma_LR). C (comparator): w = 0.10/sigma_total of the month (volatility, not variance, scaling), cap 2 x static.
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily F_ES; rf
candidates.external_evidence: Wang-Yan (9 factors + 94 anomalies): downside-vol-managed factors have positive spanning alphas for all 9 factors; real-time expanding-window tests (gamma 5, leverage <= 5): market Sharpe 0.51 vs 0.46 unmanaged vs 0.48 total-vol managed (market difference n.s., p = 0.63); 70 of 103 portfolios improve (binomial p < 0.01); fixed 50/50 weights further improve real-time results. Gain comes from return timing (high downside vol predicts low returns).
candidates.adaptation_note: ES futures instead of the CRSP market factor; volatility (not variance) scaling as in the source.

candidates.name: Conditional volatility targeting on ES (act only in extreme vol states)
sources: Bongaerts, Kang & van Dijk (2020) FAJ 76(4):54-71, Conditional Volatility Targeting, https://repub.eur.nl/pub/130215/Bongaerts-Kang-van-Dijk-Conditional-volatility-targeting-2020-FAJ.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at month-end d. RV = annualised std of daily returns in the month ending d. Breakpoints = quintiles of all prior monthly RVs (expanding, min 96 months; history prepended from ^GSPC daily 2003+ or FF Mkt-RF 1963+). Target sigma* = expanding long-run vol of daily returns x sqrt(252). Exposure in units of 1x ES notional: top quintile -> w = sigma*/RV; bottom quintile -> w = min(sigma*/RV, 2); otherwise w = 1. A as stated. B (unlevered): only the top-quintile de-levering, else 1. C: quartiles instead of quintiles.
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily F_ES; index_daily ^GSPC or ff_daily Mkt_RF for breakpoint history; rf
candidates.external_evidence: Source (10 equity markets 1982-2019, 25 bp cost of volatility-targeting trades): US Sharpe +0.16 vs buy-and-hold (significant 5%), max drawdown -8.3 pp, annual turnover 1.6 vs 2.4 for conventional targeting; 10-market average +0.07 with improvements in all markets; conventional vol targeting improves only 8 of 10 markets and can deepen drawdowns. US momentum factor Sharpe +0.17 (1% significance).
candidates.adaptation_note: Futures sample starts 2010, so the quintile history uses the S&P index before ES is available; position sizes are 1x notional (natural sizing), not 10% vol.

candidates.name: VIX-managed ES (implied-vol scaling)
sources: Bozovic (2024) IRFA 95:103353, VIX-managed portfolios (SSRN 4507634), https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finana/v95y2024ipas1057521924002850.html
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at month-end d. VIXbar = mean daily ^VIX close over the month ending d. A: w = 0.10 / (kappa x VIXbar/100), kappa = trailing 60-month median of realised next-month ES vol / month-end VIX (estimated with data up to d only), cap 2 x static. B: w = c / VIXbar^2 (variance scaling) with c set so the trailing 120-month mean weight equals the static weight, cap 2 x static. C: as A but rebalanced daily on VIX_d.
candidates.data_needed: index_daily ^VIX; futures_daily F_ES; rf
candidates.external_evidence: Bozovic (2024): scaling leverage by the previous month's VIX gives significant spanning alphas net of transaction costs across 10 equity factors, 6 mean-variance-efficient portfolio classes and 176 anomalies, with more stable weights and less leverage than realised-vol scaling; attributed to timing volatility and tail risk. No live record.
candidates.adaptation_note: Exact scaling constant in the source not verified (abstract only); kappa removes the average VRP bias of VIX.

candidates.name: Credit-spread trend equity timing (Baa spread, HYG/IEF, excess bond premium)
sources: Gilchrist & Zakrajsek (2012) AER, Credit Spreads and Business Cycle Fluctuations; EBP data https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/notes/feds-notes/ebp_csv.csv
Lopez-Salido, Stein & Zakrajsek (2017) QJE, Credit-Market Sentiment and the Business Cycle
Counterpoint Funds, https://counterpointfunds.com/high-yield-and-changes-in-credit-spread/
Counter-evidence: Insight Investment (2025), https://insightinvestment.com/globalassets/documents/us-redesign-documents/perspectives/high-yield---time-in-the-market-beats-timing-the-market-2025.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Base = long F_ES at 10% ex-ante vol. A (daily): weight 0 when BAA10Y (FRED, value dated d-1) > its trailing 126-session SMA + 0.10 percentage points, else base. B (daily): weight 0 when the 63-session total return of HYG minus that of IEF (adjusted closes at d) < 0, else base. C (monthly): using the latest EBP observation released by d (CSV value for month m usable from mid-month m+1), weight 0.5 x base when EBP > 0 and EBP minus its value 3 months earlier > 0, else base.
candidates.instruments: F_ES (signals from FRED BAA10Y, ETFs HYG/IEF, Fed EBP)
candidates.data_needed: FRED BAA10Y CSV (1986+, free); etf_daily HYG (2007-04+), IEF; Fed ebp_csv.csv (1973+); F_ES
candidates.external_evidence: GZ (2012): the excess bond premium predicts economic activity and widens ahead of recessions; Lopez-Salido et al. (2017): elevated credit-market sentiment predicts later spread widening and slowdowns. Practitioners report spread widening off low levels preceding equity peaks; Insight Investment finds high-yield range timing (buy wide/sell tight) underperforms holding. No rigorous net out-of-sample equity-timing test located.
candidates.adaptation_note: Local BAMLH0A0HYM2 only covers 2023-10 onward (FRED truncated ICE BofA history), so Moody's BAA10Y and HYG/IEF substitute for HY OAS. EBP is re-estimated each release (not point-in-time); treat C as descriptive unless vintages are archived.

candidates.name: Yield-curve inversion equity timing (10y-3m)
sources: Resnick & Shoesmith (2002) FAJ 58(3):82-90, Using the Yield Curve to Time the Stock Market, https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/research/financial-analysts-journal/2002/using-the-yield-curve-to-time-the-stock-market
Quantpedia (2022), https://quantpedia.com/avoid-equity-bear-markets-with-a-market-timing-strategy-part-3/
Counter: Carlson (2019), https://awealthofcommonsense.com/2019/08/you-probably-cant-use-the-yield-curve-to-time-the-market/
candidates.exact_rule: Base = long F_ES at 10% vol. A (daily): T-bills when T10Y3M (FRED, value dated d-1) < 0, else base. B (Resnick-Shoesmith probit, monthly): expanding probit (1971+) of a bear-market-next-month indicator (bear months = peak-to-trough S&P declines of at least 20%, labels used only once at least 24 months old) on the month-end 10y-3m spread; hold base if fitted P(bear) < 0.5 else T-bills. C (un-inversion): when the 3-month average of T10Y3M has been < 0 and then turns > 0, hold T-bills for the next 12 months; otherwise base.
candidates.data_needed: FRED T10Y3M (1982+), GS10/TB3MS monthly for 1971-1981, S&P monthly (Shiller) for labels; F_ES
candidates.external_evidence: Resnick-Shoesmith 1971-1999: switching to T-bills when P(bear next month) >= 50% earned 16.46%/yr, +229 bp/yr over S&P buy-and-hold (gross). Quantpedia 1927-2022: YC + 200-day trend + macro composite Sharpe 0.60 vs 0.35, max DD -25% vs -85% (designed in-sample). Counter: inversion lead times are too variable to time; the 2022-2024 inversion was not followed by a bear market.
candidates.adaptation_note: Few signals in 2010-2026 (inversions 2019 and 2022-2024), so low statistical power; B needs ex-post bear labels with a 24-month embargo.

candidates.name: Term-spread / forward-rate timing of 10-year note duration
sources: Campbell & Shiller (1991) RES; Fama & Bliss (1987) AER
Cochrane & Piazzesi (2005) AER, Bond Risk Premia, https://www.nber.org/papers/w9178.pdf
Counter: Thornton & Valente (2012) RFS, Out-of-sample predictions of bond excess returns and forward rates: an asset allocation perspective
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. TS = DGS10 - DTB3 (FRED, as of d-1). A: long F_ZN at 10% vol if TS > its trailing 120-month median (min 60), else flat. B: ZN weight = clip(z, -1, 1) x 10%-vol base, z = (TS - trailing 120m mean)/trailing 120m sd. C (Cochrane-Piazzesi): CP_d = gamma_hat' [y1, f2, f3, f4, f5] from FRED DGS1, DGS2, DGS3, DGS5 (forwards by linear interpolation of yields), gamma_hat from an expanding regression (min 120 months, 1976+) of the average 1-year excess holding return of 2-5y zero bonds (built from FRED yields) on those forwards; long ZN at 10% vol if CP_d > 0 else flat.
candidates.data_needed: fred_daily DGS10, DTB3, DGS2; FRED CSV DGS1, DGS3, DGS5 (free); futures_daily F_ZN
candidates.external_evidence: Fama-Bliss, Campbell-Shiller: steep curves/forward spreads predict positive bond excess returns; Cochrane-Piazzesi: a single forward-rate factor explains up to 44% of 1-year bond excess return variance in-sample (1964-2003). Thornton-Valente (2012): out of sample these predictors give no economic value to a mean-variance bond investor vs the expectations hypothesis.
candidates.adaptation_note: Overlaps the edge-search curve-carry series (carry_ts_rates); report correlation with it.

candidates.name: Fed policy regime (expansive vs restrictive) allocation
sources: Jensen, Mercer & Johnson (1996) JFE, Business conditions, monetary policy, and expected security returns
Conover, Jensen, Johnson & Mercer (2005) FAJ 61(1):70-79, Is Fed Policy Still Relevant for Investors?, https://ideas.repec.org/a/taf/ufajxx/v61y2005i1p70-79.html
Jensen, Johnson & Mercer (2000) CFA Research Foundation, https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/research/foundation/2000/the-role-of-monetary-policy-in-investment-management
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. Regime = direction of the most recent change in the Fed target rate known at d (FRED DFEDTAR to 2008-12-15, DFEDTARU after): expansive if the last change was a cut, restrictive if a hike. A: expansive -> F_ES at 10% vol, restrictive -> T-bills. B: expansive -> ES 1.0 x base, restrictive -> 0.5 x base. C: expansive -> F_ES, restrictive -> F_ZN (each 10% vol).
candidates.data_needed: FRED DFEDTAR, DFEDTARU (free); F_ES, F_ZN
candidates.external_evidence: JMJ (1954-1992) and Conover et al. (38 years of US data): stock returns are consistently higher and less volatile in expansive regimes; Conover et al. (2007) cyclical-sector rotation in expansive periods 1973-2005 +3.78%/yr gross. Post-2008 evidence untested; only five regime changes in 2010-2026 (2008-12 cut, 2015-12 hike, 2019-07 cut, 2022-03 hike, 2024-09 cut).
candidates.adaptation_note: Very low number of regime switches in our sample; restrictive periods 2016-2019 and 2022-2024 contain strong equity years.

candidates.name: Relative T-bill rate (short-rate trend) equity timing
sources: Ang & Bekaert (2007) RFS 20(3):651-707, Stock Return Predictability: Is it There?, https://business.columbia.edu/sites/default/files-efs/imce-uploads/gbekaert/papers/stockreturn.pdf
Campbell (1991) EJ relative bill rate
Counter: Goyal & Welch (2008) RFS; Goyal, Welch & Zafirov (2024) RFS
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. RREL = DTB3 (as of d-1) minus its mean over the trailing 252 sessions. A: F_ES weight = 1.0 x 10%-vol base if RREL <= 0, else 0.5 x base. B: weight = clip(1 - RREL/1.0pp, 0, 1.5) x base. C: same as A with the 126-session change in DGS2 replacing RREL.
candidates.data_needed: fred_daily DTB3, DGS2; F_ES
candidates.external_evidence: Ang-Bekaert: the short rate is the only robust short-horizon (negative) predictor of equity returns across the US, UK, Germany, France and Japan (in-sample, robust to small-sample bias). Goyal-Welch: T-bill-based predictors perform poorly out of sample in US data.
candidates.adaptation_note: Zero-lower-bound period 2010-2015 gives RREL near zero (mostly fully invested).

candidates.name: US macro momentum (growth, inflation, policy, risk, dollar trends) for ES and ZN
sources: Brooks (2017) AQR, A Half Century of Macro Momentum, https://smallake.kr/wp-content/uploads/2017/10/A-Half-Century-of-Macro-Momentum.pdf
https://www.aqr.com/library/aqr-publications/a-half-century-of-macro-momentum
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d with data released by d. Theme changes, each divided by its trailing 120-month std (min 60): G = -(UNRATE latest - UNRATE 12 months earlier); I = CPI YoY latest - CPI YoY 12 months earlier (CPIAUCNS); M = -(DGS2_d - DGS2 252 sessions earlier) (expansionary = positive); R = trailing 252-session F_ES excess return; X = trailing 252-session USD return (UUP, or minus the equal-weight return of the 6 FX futures). Equity score S_E = (G - I + M + R - X)/5; bond score S_B = (-G - I - M - R + X)/5 (source signs). A: F_ES and F_ZN each at 10% vol x clip(S, -1, 1), equal risk. B: long-only (clip(S, 0, 1)). C: bond sleeve only.
candidates.instruments: F_ES, F_ZN (signals from FRED UNRATE, CPIAUCNS, DGS2; UUP or FX futures)
candidates.data_needed: FRED UNRATE, CPIAUCNS (release dates: CPI mid-month, UNRATE first Friday); fred_daily DGS2; etf_daily UUP; futures F_ES, F_ZN, FX
candidates.external_evidence: Brooks (2017, cross-country, 4 asset classes, 5 themes): 1970-2016 excess return 13.0%/yr, vol 10.7%, Sharpe 1.2 gross; positive in every decade (2010-2016 Sharpe 0.7); bonds sleeve Sharpe 0.5, equities 0.7; correlation with S&P -0.22; gained in each of the five largest equity drawdowns. Hypothetical and gross of costs.
candidates.adaptation_note: The source is cross-sectional across countries; a US-only directional version is our adaptation and untested by the source. UNRATE and CPI NSA are rarely revised, so current vintages are near point-in-time.

candidates.name: Growth/inflation quadrant regime allocation
sources: Ilmanen, Maloney & Ross (2014) JPM, Exploring Macroeconomic Sensitivities: How Investments Respond to Different Economic Environments
Neville, Draaisma, Funnell, Harvey & Van Hemert (2021) JPM 47(8), The Best Strategies for Inflationary Times, https://www.evidenceinvestor.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/SSRN-id3813202.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. Growth up if UNRATE (latest released) < its 12-month SMA; inflation up if CPI YoY (CPIAUCNS, latest released) > its 12-month SMA. Sleeves each at 10% vol: EQ = F_ES; BD = F_ZN; CM = equal-risk basket of CL, HO, NG, HG, GC, SI, ZC, ZS, ZW, LE; GD = F_GC. A (switch): growth up/inflation down -> EQ; growth up/inflation up -> 50% EQ + 50% CM; growth down/inflation down -> BD; growth down/inflation up -> 50% GD + 50% T-bills. B (tilt): equal-risk base of EQ, BD, CM, GD with the quadrant's favoured sleeves doubled, renormalised to 10% portfolio vol. C: as A with market signals (growth = sign of 126-session change in the HG/GC price ratio; inflation = sign of 126-session change in T10YIE).
candidates.instruments: F_ES, F_ZN, F_GC, commodity futures basket
candidates.data_needed: FRED UNRATE, CPIAUCNS, T10YIE (2003+); futures_daily; databento front closes for the HG/GC ratio
candidates.external_evidence: Ilmanen-Maloney-Ross (1972-2013): equities do best when growth is rising, nominal bonds when growth falls, commodities when inflation rises (contemporaneous sorts). Neville et al. (US/UK/Japan, about 95 years): unexpected inflation hurts bonds and equities; commodities positive in inflation surges; trend following most reliable. Regime sorts are contemporaneous; no published lagged-signal net trading record.
candidates.adaptation_note: Lagged release-date signals replace contemporaneous regime labels; expect much weaker results than the source sorts.

candidates.name: Stock-bond correlation regime switching in risk parity
sources: Brixton, Brooks, Hecht, Ilmanen, Maloney & McQuinn (2023) JPM, A Changing Stock-Bond Correlation: Drivers and Implications, https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/A-Changing-Stock-Bond-Correlation
Empirical Evidence on the Stock-Bond Correlation (2024), https://top1000funds.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Empirical-Evidence-on-the-Stock-Bond-Correlation.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. Base = equal-risk F_ES + F_ZN levered to 10% vol with the trailing 252-session covariance. rho = correlation of daily ES and ZN excess returns over the trailing 126 sessions. A: if rho > 0, the ZN risk budget goes to T-bills (ES keeps its half-risk weight). B: if rho > 0, the ZN budget goes to F_GC (inverse-vol weight). C: ZN weight multiplied by clip(1 - 2 rho, 0, 1), then the portfolio is re-scaled to 10% vol.
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily F_ES, F_ZN, F_GC; rf
candidates.external_evidence: AQR: a model based on the relative volatility of growth and inflation explains about 70% of long-term variation in the US stock-bond correlation (less of short-term moves); positive-correlation regimes (pre-2000, 2022+) remove bond diversification; suggests adding alternatives/commodities when inflation uncertainty is high. No published net trading test of a switching rule found.
candidates.adaptation_note: Compare with the edge-search static stock/bond sleeve rpm_SB_STATIC (same base construction).

candidates.name: Growth-Trend Timing (unemployment trend gates a 10-month trend filter)
sources: Philosophical Economics (2016), Growth and Trend, https://www.philosophicaleconomics.com/?p=6785 and https://www.philosophicaleconomics.com/?p=7644
Keller (2019) via CXO, https://www.cxoadvisory.com/equity-premium/optimizing-the-combination-of-economic-growth-and-price-trends/
Newfound Research, https://blog.thinknewfound.com/tag/gtt/
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at the last session d of month m. U = UNRATE for month m-1 (released first Friday of m; if not yet released at d use m-2). Unemployment trend up if U > mean of the 12 latest monthly values. Price trend down if F_ES TR month-end close at d < mean of the last 10 month-end closes. Hold F_ES at 10% vol unless (unemployment trend up AND price trend down), then T-bills. A as stated. B: growth flag = ICSA 4-week average > its 52-week average (weekly, Thursday release). C: growth flag = SAHMREALTIME >= 0.30.
candidates.data_needed: FRED UNRATE, ICSA, SAHMREALTIME (free); futures_daily F_ES
candidates.external_evidence: Philosophical Economics: 1930-2016 GTT beat buy-and-hold and the plain 10-month SMA by more than 150 bp/yr, also on unrevised data from 1961. Keller (2019) out-of-sample Jul 1981-Oct 2019: CAGR 9.8% vs 8.5% for 60/40 with lower max drawdown, but large subperiod dispersion. Newfound: growth-trend reduces whipsaw in international tests.
candidates.adaptation_note: Our faber/GTAA test (S3) is the plain-trend control; GTT differs only when unemployment is falling (stays long through trend breaks).

candidates.name: Kaminski-Lo stop-loss: equities to Treasuries on cumulative losses
sources: Kaminski & Lo (2014) JFM 18:234-254, When Do Stop-Loss Rules Stop Losses?, https://chesler.us/resources/academia/stop%20losses.pdf, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=968338
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at month-end d. R_J = sum of the last J monthly excess returns of unlevered F_ES. State s: if invested and R_J < -gamma -> switch to the stop asset at next_close; if stopped and the last month's ES excess return >= delta -> re-enter. Exposure when invested = F_ES at 10% vol; stop asset = F_ZN at 10% vol (source: long-term government bonds). A: J = 12, gamma = 8%, delta = 0%, stop asset ZN. B: same, stop asset T-bills. C: J = 6, gamma = 6%, delta = 0%, stop asset ZN.
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily F_ES, F_ZN; rf
candidates.external_evidence: Kaminski-Lo 1950-2004 monthly (CRSP VW, Ibbotson LT govt bonds): with J = 12, gamma = 8%, delta = 0, 37 stops (about 0.9/yr) and 50 stopped-out months; during stop-outs equities earned 4.5%/yr vs bonds 15.6%/yr; certain rules add 50-100 bp/month during stop-out periods. Single study, gross, relies on flight-to-quality (negative stock-bond correlation).
candidates.adaptation_note: Thresholds applied to unlevered ES returns to match the source's index scale; the 2022 positive stock-bond correlation is a known failure case.

candidates.name: Grossman-Zhou drawdown-floor exposure control
sources: Grossman & Zhou (1993) Mathematical Finance, Optimal investment strategies for controlling drawdowns
Chekhlov, Uryasev & Zabarankin (2005) J. Risk, Drawdown measure in portfolio optimization
candidates.exact_rule: Daily on the strategy's own NAV V (base = F_ES at 10% vol). HWM_d = running max of V. Multiplier m_d = clip(k x (1 - (1 - D) x HWM_d / V_d), 0, 1) applied to the base position. A: D = 20%, k = 5 (full exposure at the high-water mark, zero at a 20% drawdown). B: D = 15%, k = 6.67. C: as A with HWM = trailing 252-session max of V (avoids permanent lock-out).
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily F_ES; rf
candidates.external_evidence: Theory: Grossman-Zhou show the optimal policy under a max-drawdown constraint invests in proportion to the cushion above a fraction of the running maximum. No out-of-sample net evidence of Sharpe improvement found; known issues are path dependence and cash lock after deep drawdowns.
candidates.adaptation_note: Pure risk-control overlay; expected value is drawdown reduction, not Sharpe.

candidates.name: Financial turbulence (Mahalanobis) exposure filter
sources: Kritzman & Li (2010) FAJ 66(5):30-41, Skulls, Financial Turbulence, and Risk Management, https://rpc.cfainstitute.org/research/financial-analysts-journal/2010/skulls-financial-turbulence-and-risk-management
Kritzman, Page & Turkington (2012) FAJ, Regime Shifts: Implications for Dynamic Strategies
Replication: https://portfoliooptimizer.io/blog/the-turbulence-index-measuring-financial-risk/
Code: https://github.com/luigi-piva/turbulence-index
candidates.exact_rule: Daily. r_t = daily excess returns of F_ES, F_RTY, F_ZN, F_ZB, F_CL, F_GC, F_HG, F_6E, F_6J, F_ZC. d_t = (r_t - mu)' Sigma^-1 (r_t - mu) / 10 with mu, Sigma from the trailing 756 sessions ending t-1. s_t = mean of d over the last 5 sessions; P_t = percentile of s_t within its trailing 756-session history. Base = F_ES at 10% vol. A: weight 0 when P_t > 75%, else base. B: weight = base x (1 - P_t). C: weight 0.5 x base when P_t > 75%.
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily (10 roots listed); rf
candidates.external_evidence: Kritzman-Li: returns to risky assets are much lower in turbulent periods regardless of source; turbulence is persistent; used as an exposure filter for risky strategies. Kritzman-Page-Turkington: Markov regimes on turbulence, inflation and growth improve dynamic allocations. Replication (Apr 2009-Mar 2022, weekly, 7 asset classes): turbulence-scaled US equities Sharpe about 2.2 vs about 1.0 buy-and-hold at about 50% average exposure (likely optimistic, single run).
candidates.adaptation_note: Futures replace the 7 asset-class indices; 75th-percentile threshold follows the common application of the source.

candidates.name: Absorption ratio systemic-risk stock/bond switch
sources: Kritzman, Li, Page & Rigobon (2011) JPM, Principal Components as a Measure of Systemic Risk, https://globalmarkets.statestreet.com/research/portal/insights/article/2a8e282a-343b-443c-b362-1634c71d2d26
Code: https://github.com/hugogobato/Absorption_ratio-Mark-Kritzman-Yuanzhen-Li-Sebastien-Page-Roberto-Rigobon-2010-
candidates.exact_rule: Daily. Daily returns of the 9 sector SPDRs (XLB XLE XLF XLI XLK XLP XLU XLV XLY); exponentially weighted covariance over 500 sessions (half-life 250). AR_t = sum of the 2 largest eigenvalues / trace. dAR_t = (mean AR last 15 sessions - mean AR last 252) / std of AR over last 252. A: dAR > +1 -> 100% F_ZN at 10% vol; dAR < -1 -> 100% F_ES at 10% vol; otherwise 50/50 equal-risk ES/ZN. B: F_ES only, flat when dAR > +1. C: universe = the 30 futures with 6 eigenvectors.
candidates.data_needed: etf_daily XL* sectors (2003+); futures_daily F_ES, F_ZN
candidates.external_evidence: KLPR: most significant US drawdowns were preceded by absorption-ratio spikes; stocks fell on average after dAR > 1 and rose after dAR < -1; the original article reports the dynamic stock/bond strategy beating a static 50/50 mix (exact figures not verified here).
candidates.adaptation_note: 9 sector ETFs replace 51 MSCI US industries (eigenvector count = 1/5 of assets, rounded up).

candidates.name: Low-volatility / low-beta sector allocation
sources: Baker, Bradley & Taliaferro (2014) FAJ 70(2), The Low-Risk Anomaly: A Decomposition into Micro and Macro Effects, https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2210003
Frazzini & Pedersen (2014) JFE 111(1), Betting Against Beta, http://docs.lhpedersen.com/BettingAgainstBeta.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d, 9 sector SPDRs, adjusted closes. A (long-only defensive): equal-weight the 3 sectors with the lowest trailing 252-session vol; scale the portfolio to 10% ex-ante vol (EWMA covariance, gross cap 2). B (sector BAB): beta vs SPY = corr(1260d, 3-day returns) x vol ratio (252d), shrunk 0.6 beta + 0.4; rank-weighted low-beta leg scaled to beta 1 long, high-beta leg scaled to beta 1 short; scale to 10% vol; shorts pay 30 bp/yr. C: long-only minimum variance across the 9 sectors (trailing 252d covariance, Ledoit-Wolf), scaled to 10% vol.
candidates.instruments: XLB XLE XLF XLI XLK XLP XLU XLV XLY, SPY
candidates.data_needed: etf_daily (2003+); config.cost_bps
candidates.external_evidence: Baker-Bradley-Taliaferro: the low-beta anomaly has a macro component from choosing low-beta industries and countries in addition to stock selection. Frazzini-Pedersen: BAB delivers positive risk-adjusted returns across equity markets, bonds, credit and futures. Live record: S&P 500 Low Volatility index (2011 launch) and low-vol ETFs have run with lower volatility than the S&P 500 for more than a decade (not quantified here).
candidates.adaptation_note: Sector ETFs are a coarse universe (9 assets); report beta-adjusted alpha vs SPY.

candidates.name: Betting against beta on the Treasury futures curve
sources: Frazzini & Pedersen (2014) JFE 111(1):1-25, Betting Against Beta, Table 6, http://docs.lhpedersen.com/BettingAgainstBeta.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. Assets F_ZT, F_ZF, F_ZN, F_ZB, F_UB. Market = equal-weight of the 5. beta_i = corr(1260 sessions, 3-day overlapping returns) x sigma_i/sigma_m (252 sessions), shrunk 0.6 beta + 0.4. z = rank(beta), k = 2 / sum |z - zbar|, w_H = k (z - zbar)+, w_L = k (z - zbar)-. BAB = (1/beta_L) w_L'r - (1/beta_H) w_H'r. A: BAB scaled to 10% ex-ante vol with gross cap 6. B: two-leg long ZT / short ZB, beta-neutral, scaled to 10% vol. C: as A with gross cap 4.
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily Treasury roots; rf
candidates.external_evidence: Frazzini-Pedersen, CRSP Treasury portfolios Jan 1952-Mar 2012: Treasury BAB 0.17%/month (t = 6.26), Sharpe 0.81; portfolio Sharpe ratios fall monotonically from 0.73 (1-12 month maturities) to 0.31 (>10 years). No futures-based post-2012 record found.
candidates.adaptation_note: Large ZT leverage (5-8x notional) needed; gross cap matters, so A and C differ only in the cap. Related to curve carry (carry_xs_rates).

candidates.name: Dollar carry trade (average forward discount timing of the USD)
sources: Lustig, Roussanov & Verdelhan (2014) JFE 111(3):527-553, Countercyclical Currency Risk Premia, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w16427/revisions/w16427.rev1.pdf
Quantpedia summary, https://quantpedia.com/strategies/dollar-carry-trade
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. For each FX future i in {6E, 6J, 6B, 6A, 6C, 6S}: carry_i = ln(F_front / F_second) x 12 / (months between the two expiries) (approximately foreign minus US short rate; from databento .v.0/.v.1 closes and free symbology for expiries). AFD = mean of carry_i. A: AFD > 0 -> long the equal-risk basket of the 6 FX futures (short USD), AFD < 0 -> short the basket; scale to 10% vol. B: same with AFD from FRED 3-month interbank rates (OECD IR3TIB01 series for EA, JP, GB, AU, CA, CH, one-month publication lag) minus DTB3. C: position = clip(AFD / 1%, -1, 1) x 10%-vol basket.
candidates.instruments: F_6E, F_6J, F_6B, F_6A, F_6C, F_6S
candidates.data_needed: databento_raw glbx_ohlcv1d (front/second closes + instrument_id symbology); FRED IR3TIB01 series (free); futures_daily FX
candidates.external_evidence: LRV: dollar carry (long all foreign currencies when the average forward discount is positive, short otherwise) on developed currencies 1983-2009: about 5.6%/yr, vol 8.5%, Sharpe 0.66, max DD -32%; AFD and US IP growth forecast up to 25% of 1-year dollar return variation; nearly uncorrelated with cross-sectional carry. Post-publication record not verified.
candidates.adaptation_note: 6 currencies vs the source's 10-15; carry from futures basis. Distinct from the edge-search per-currency series carry_ts_fx (aggregate sign vs per-currency sign); report correlation.

candidates.name: Commodity currencies forecast commodity prices
sources: Chen, Rogoff & Rossi (2010) QJE 125(3):1145-1194, Can Exchange Rates Forecast Commodity Prices?, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w13901/w13901.pdf, https://www.nber.org/digest/jul08/w13901.html
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. S = mean of the trailing 63-session excess returns of F_6A and F_6C. Basket = equal-risk long of CL, HO, RB, NG, GC, SI, PL, HG, ZC, ZS, ZW, ZL, ZM, LE, HE scaled to 10% vol. A: long basket if S > 0, else flat. B: long if S > 0, short if S < 0. C: as A with a 21-session S.
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily; rf
candidates.external_evidence: Chen-Rogoff-Rossi (quarterly, commodity currencies of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, Chile; samples of one to three decades to 2008): exchange rates robustly forecast country commodity indices and the IMF world commodity index in and out of sample; the reverse direction fails out of sample. Statistical forecast evidence, not a net trading record.
candidates.adaptation_note: Two currencies (AUD, CAD) available vs five in the source; monthly rebalance of a quarterly-horizon signal.

candidates.name: Gold/copper ratio trend for 10-year note timing
sources: Kaeppel (2021) SentimenTrader, Using Metals to Trade Bonds, https://sentimentrader.com/blog/using-metals-to-trade-bonds
Oort (2020) Erasmus thesis, https://thesis.eur.nl/pub/53697/BSc-Thesis-Sebastiaan-Oort-Final-version.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Daily. A_d = GC front-month close / HG front-month close (raw unadjusted front closes from databento glbx_ohlcv1d .v.0). D_d = SMA30(A) - SMA80(A). A: long F_ZN at 10% vol if D_d >= 0, else flat. B: long if D_d >= 0, short otherwise. C (monthly): long ZN if the 126-session change in HG/GC is negative, else flat.
candidates.data_needed: databento_raw glbx_ohlcv1d (GC, HG front closes); futures_daily F_ZN
candidates.external_evidence: Kaeppel, May 1982-Apr 2021, 10-year note futures: +$110,072 per contract held only when the gold/copper 30-day MA >= 80-day MA vs -$40,017 when below (no costs). Oort (1988-2020): the copper/gold ratio significantly predicts the 10-year yield after macro controls, including out-of-sample tests; relationship reported weaker after 2020.
candidates.adaptation_note: Roll jumps in raw front closes affect the ratio slightly; use a back-adjusted ratio of the two TR indices as a check.

candidates.name: Oil price changes predict equity returns (striking oil)
sources: Driesprong, Jacobsen & Maat (2008) JFE 89(2), Striking Oil: Another Puzzle?, https://repub.eur.nl/pub/1017

Narayan & Gupta (2015) Energy Economics, Has oil price predicted stock returns for over a century?, https://dro.deakin.edu.au/articles/journal_contribution/Has_oil_price_predicted_stock_returns_for_over_a_century_/20915227/1
Counter: https://www.capitalspectator.com/?p=4128
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at month-end d. r_oil = F_CL TR excess return over the calendar month ending d. A: F_ES weight = 1.0 x 10%-vol base if r_oil <= 0, else 0.5 x base. B: expanding OLS (min 60 months; history from FRED MCOILWTICO and S&P monthly from 1983) of next-month S&P excess return on r_oil; weight 1.0 if forecast > 0 else 0.25. C: as A using the 3-month oil return.
candidates.data_needed: futures_daily F_CL, F_ES; FRED MCOILWTICO for regression history
candidates.external_evidence: Driesprong et al. (monthly, 1973-2003, 18 developed markets): oil price changes significantly and negatively predict next-month returns in 12 of 18 markets and the world index; a 10% oil drop roughly doubles the next-month US expected return; robust to January/Halloween effects; emerging markets supply out-of-sample support. Narayan-Gupta (1859-2013): in- and out-of-sample predictability. Capital Spectator: weak in recent decades.
candidates.adaptation_note: Sign of the oil-equity relation flipped to positive in demand-driven episodes (2008-2015, 2020), a known risk.

candidates.name: CAPE value + 12-month momentum equity tilt (sin a little)
sources: Asness, Ilmanen & Maloney (2017) JOIM 15(3), Market Timing: Sin a Little, https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Insights/White-Papers/Market-Timing-Sin-a-Little.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. EP = 1/CAPE from Shiller ie_data (value for month m-1). Value tilt V = 1 + (EP_trim - median EP)/(P95 - P5), EP trimmed at the 5th/95th percentiles, percentiles over an expanding window from 1881 until 60 years are available and a rolling 60-year window after; clip [0.5, 1.5]. Momentum tilt Mo = same transform applied to the trailing 12-month S&P excess return. A: ES weight = (0.5 V + 0.5 Mo) x 10%-vol base. B: V only. C: Mo only.
candidates.data_needed: Shiller ie_data (CAPE, S&P total return monthly; current copy needed for 2024-2026); futures_daily F_ES
candidates.external_evidence: AIM (1900-2015, gross): value timing Sharpe 0.37 vs buy-and-hold 0.38 (1958-2015: 0.37 vs 0.37); momentum timing 0.48 vs 0.38; value+momentum 0.43 vs 0.38 (1958-2015: 0.41 vs 0.37), max drawdown -80% vs -83%; neither value-only difference significant.
candidates.adaptation_note: The momentum half overlaps our 12-month TSMOM tests; value-only is the distinct piece. The Shiller file at the old URL was last saved 2024-09.

candidates.name: Combination equity-premium forecast (Rapach-Strauss-Zhou) market timing
sources: Rapach, Strauss & Zhou (2010) RFS 23(2):821-862, Out-of-Sample Equity Premium Prediction: Combination Forecasts and Links to the Real Economy, https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v23y2010i2p821-862.html
Goyal, Welch & Zafirov (2024) RFS 37(11), https://www.ivo-welch.org/home/card-eqpredict.html
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. Predictors (each lagged to release): D/P and E/P (Shiller, 1-month lag), T-bill rate, long yield (GS10), term spread (GS10 - TB3MS), default yield spread (BAA - AAA, FRED), inflation (CPI YoY, 1-month lag), stock variance (sum of squared daily S&P returns in the month). For each predictor: expanding OLS (start 1947 or first data, min 120 months) of next-month S&P excess return on the predictor -> forecast f_k. f = combination of f_k. Weight on F_ES (1 = 1x notional) = clip(f / (3 sigma2), 0, 1.5), sigma2 = trailing 60-month variance of monthly excess returns. A: mean combination. B: median combination. C: discounted-MSPE combination (theta = 0.9, 40-quarter holdout as in RSZ adapted to 120 months).
candidates.data_needed: Shiller ie_data; FRED TB3MS, GS10, BAA, AAA, CPIAUCNS (free); Goyal predictor file (free) for cross-check; futures_daily F_ES
candidates.external_evidence: RSZ: combination forecasts deliver statistically and economically significant out-of-sample gains over the historical mean, consistently over time (quarterly 1965-2005; mean-combination out-of-sample R2 about 3.6%, utility gains of a few percent per year for risk aversion 3). Goyal-Welch-Zafirov (data to 2021): most individual predictors lost support; only a handful (e.g. accruals, short interest, CEP, technical NRTZ) still work in- and out-of-sample.
candidates.adaptation_note: Predictor set restricted to free FRED/Shiller series; monthly instead of quarterly.

candidates.name: Chicago Fed financial-conditions (NFCI) weekly-change timing
sources: CXO Advisory (2020), Exploiting Chicago Fed NFCI Predictive Power, https://www.cxoadvisory.com/economic-indicators/exploiting-chicago-fed-nfsi-predictive-power/
Data: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NFCI
candidates.exact_rule: Weekly. NFCI for the week ending Friday F is released the following Wednesday 8:30 ET. At the close of release day d: dN = NFCI_F - NFCI_(F - 1 week) from the vintage available at d. A: hold F_ES at 10% vol from next_close until the next release if dN < mean of all prior weekly changes (expanding from 1971), else T-bills. B: threshold = mean + 1 sd. C: ANFCI instead of NFCI.
candidates.data_needed: FRED NFCI/ANFCI (current vintage free; ALFRED vintages needed for point-in-time); futures_daily F_ES
candidates.external_evidence: CXO, Feb 1993-Apr 2020 SPY: A CAGR 11.8%, B 11.7% vs 10.4% buy-and-hold; B max drawdown about 38% vs 55%; both avoided most of the 2008-09 crash, only A avoided 2001-02. CXO warns results changed materially between iterations because of weekly renormalisation and model revisions.
candidates.adaptation_note: Current-vintage NFCI has look-ahead from renormalisation; use ALFRED vintage downloads or label results descriptive.

candidates.name: Real-yield and breakeven signals for gold and commodities
sources: Erb & Harvey (2013) FAJ, The Golden Dilemma; coverage https://people.duke.edu/~charvey/Media/2013/WSJ_June_28_2013.pdf
candidates.exact_rule: Monthly at d. A: long F_GC at 10% vol if the 63-session change in DFII10 (10-year TIPS real yield, FRED as of d-1) < 0, else flat. B: A AND the 63-session UUP return < 0 (weak dollar). C (breakeven regime): long the equal-risk basket CL, HO, RB, HG, ZC, ZS, ZW at 10% vol if the 63-session change in T10YIE > 0, else flat.
candidates.data_needed: FRED DFII10, T10YIE (2003+, free); etf_daily UUP; futures_daily
candidates.external_evidence: Erb-Harvey: correlation about -0.82 between real yields and gold 1997-2012 (contemporaneous, levels R2 above 0.72); the link broke in 2022-2024 when gold rallied with real yields. No evidence that lagged real-yield changes predict gold returns.
candidates.adaptation_note: Contemporaneous relation recast as a lagged momentum signal; low prior.
